article_title: Strengthening patient safety competencies among physician interns through a structured quality and safety course.
citation: Qureshi Muhammad Fazal Hussain; Asif Fozia; Khan Shahmeer Raza; Akhtar Munazza; Shah Muzna; Altaf Ahmed; Latif Asad. (2026). Strengthening patient safety competencies among physician interns through a structured quality and safety course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09875-4
title: Structured Quality and Patient Safety (QPS) module for postgraduate medical interns
description: A compulsory module in the internship curriculum at a private tertiary care hospital in Pakistan, consisting of "a pre-module online assessment administered through the institutional Virtual Learning Environment, followed by two consecutive in-person teaching days (13 contact hours)". Morning didactic lectures cover quality and patient safety, the science of safety, error disclosure, safety culture, and conflict management, followed by facilitated group-based applied learning including case-based learning on learning from defects, a communication lab, and structured case-based discussions, concluding with a post-module assessment.
requirements: Delivered as a compulsory component of the internship curriculum with pre- and post-module assessments administered through the institutional Virtual Learning Environment
constraints: The one-arm quasi-experimental design precluded a concurrent control group and limits causal attribution of observed gains
target_learners: Postgraduate medical interns in a one-year internship programme at a tertiary care hospital
target_learning_goals: Knowledge efficacy for safety and quality improvement practices
examples: Two consecutive in-person teaching days with 13 contact hours combining didactic lectures and applied learning activities such as case-based learning exercises and a communication lab
key_sources: Qureshi Muhammad Fazal Hussain; Asif Fozia; Khan Shahmeer Raza; Akhtar Munazza; Shah Muzna; Altaf Ahmed; Latif Asad. (2026). Strengthening patient safety competencies among physician interns through a structured quality and safety course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09875-4

article_title: Quantum Games and Interactive Tools for Quantum Technologies Outreach and Education
citation: Zeki C. Seskir, Piotr Migdał, Carrie Weidner, Aditya Anupam, Nicky Case, Noah Davis, Chiara Decaroli, İlke Ercan, Caterina Foti, Paweł Gora, Klementyna Jankiewicz, Brian R. La Cour, Jorge Yago Malo, Sabrina Maniscalco, Azad Naeemi, Laurentiu Nita, Nassim Parvin, Fabio Scafirimuto, Jacob F. Sherson, Elif Surer, James Wootton, Lia Yeh, Olga Zabello, Marilù Chiofaloi. (2022). Quantum Games and Interactive Tools for Quantum Technologies Outreach and Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.08519
title: QPlayLearn online platform for multi-level quantum science education
description: QPlayLearn is an online platform offering multi-level quantum science and technologies education; its stated mission is "to provide multi -level education on quantum science and technologies to anyone, regardless of age and background". Inspired by the theory of multiple intelligences, it uses a three-step method — building intuition through games and videos, understanding concepts through accessible descriptions, and acquiring formal understanding through mathematics — organized in sections Play, Discover, Learn, Apply, and Imagine, with Quest as its quantum dictionary. The article presents it as a strategy for cultural change across social strata.
requirements: The article states the effectiveness of the QPlayLearn approach needs to be assessed by means of physics education research tools in on-purpose designed experiments
constraints: Developments such as completing the quest environments and adding a multiple language version are still underway
target_learning_goals: conceptual and formal understanding of quantum science
examples: Quest, the QPlayLearn quantum dictionary, composes each entry of sections exploiting different learning approaches, letting each user begin from the approach that feels easier to them

article_title: Quantum Picturalism: Learning Quantum Theory in High School
citation: Selma D¨undar-Coecke, Lia Yeh, Caterina Puca, Sieglinde M.-L. Pfaendler, Muhammad Hamza Waseem, Thomas Cervoni, Aleks Kissinger, Stefano Gogioso, Bob Coecke. (2023). Quantum Picturalism: Learning Quantum Theory in High School. https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.03653
title: Preregistered 10-week online QP pilot intervention trial with 75 UK high-school students and post-test evaluation
description: The article details a preregistered intervention trial delivered online through weekly one-hour sessions with half an hour of self-study, spanning 10 weeks, evaluated with a post-test design. "A purposive sampling approach was employed to recruit 75 volunteer high-school students aged 16 to 19", selected from 734 applicants via random subsampling balanced on diversity criteria, with a goal of around 50 completers. Outcome variables focus on the number of problems students solve using QP, marked against a rubric covering methodology, correctness, conciseness, originality/creativity, evidence of understanding, and structuring/communication; analyses planned include ANOVA, hierarchical regressions, path analyses, multilevel modelling and exploratory factor analysis.
requirements: Tutors with DBS checks and a one-hour training session; weekly tutor feedback forms; attendance at tutorials and completion of post-testing required for data inclusion.
constraints: Sample size was determined by the number of available tutors; the article notes more evidence will be needed with diverse control groups and larger samples.
target_learners: volunteer UK high-school students aged 16 to 19
target_learning_goals: solving quantum information problems using diagrammatic methods
assessing changes in attitudes toward STEM careers
examples: Two experienced PIs independently marked exam submissions blind to each other's grades, with a third PI arbitrating discrepancies of more than 9%.
key_sources: Selma D¨undar-Coecke, Lia Yeh, Caterina Puca, Sieglinde M.-L. Pfaendler, Muhammad Hamza Waseem, Thomas Cervoni, Aleks Kissinger, Stefano Gogioso, Bob Coecke. (2023). Quantum Picturalism: Learning Quantum Theory in High School. https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.03653

article_title: Making sense of quantum teleportation: An intervention study on students' conceptions using a diagrammatic approach
citation: Sebastian Kilde-Westberg, Andreas Johansson, Anna Pearson, and Jonas Enger. (2025). Making sense of quantum teleportation: An intervention study on students' conceptions using a diagrammatic approach. arXiv:2511.21443 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21443
title: QPic-based two-lesson intervention teaching quantum teleportation with wires and boxes
description: The intervention taught quantum teleportation using QPic, a simplified diagrammatic formalism adapted from ZX-calculus in which quantum processes appear as diagrams of wires and boxes. 'The study was designed as a two-lesson intervention study': lesson one paired a 30 minute lecture with a first problem set, and lesson two a 15 minute lecture with 20 minutes of group work on exercises E1 and E2, separated by one week. A pre- and post-test gauged difficulty, with a mean difficulty rating of 6.3 out of 10.
requirements: Before students apply the formalism, 'some fundamental rules need to be established, along with necessary building blocks' — wires, boxes, type-matching, only connections matter, and time flowing upward in diagrams.
constraints: The article states the intervention 'did not focus much on connecting the diagrammatic representation of entanglement (the cup-state) to physical experimental situations' beyond a brief discussion.
target_learners: third-year upper-secondary physics students in an elective advanced physics course
target_learning_goals: understanding the principle of quantum teleportation
relating diagrammatic mathematical operations to quantum processes such as entanglement and measurement
examples: Students worked on E1, completing a diagram equality and adding error and correction boxes with a classical communication wire, and on E2, describing an experiment, reconstructing its diagram, and judging whether teleportation is faster or slower than light
key_sources: Sebastian Kilde-Westberg, Andreas Johansson, Anna Pearson, and Jonas Enger. (2025). Making sense of quantum teleportation: An intervention study on students' conceptions using a diagrammatic approach. arXiv:2511.21443 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21443

article_title: High schoolers excel at Oxford quantum course using pictorial mathematics
citation: Bob Coecke, Aleks Kissinger, Stefano Gogioso, Selma Dündar-Coecke, Caterina Puca, Lia Yeh, Muhammad Hamza Waseem, Emmanuel M. Pothos, Sieglinde Pfaendler, Vincent Wang-Mascianica, Thomas Cervoni, Ferdi Tomassini, Vincent Anandraj, Peter Sigrist and Ilyas Khan. (2025). High schoolers excel at Oxford quantum course using pictorial mathematics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00141
title: Eight-week taught course with weekly video lectures, small-group tutorials and a take-home exam modelled on a postgraduate course
description: The course structure was based roughly on that of an Oxford University postgraduate course: "an eight-week taught portion, with lectures, tutorials, and weekly exercises, followed by a take-home exam". Students watched one video lecture per week, then attended hour-long tutorial sessions in groups of up to 15 students where a tutor facilitated discussion and exercise work. The exam mirrored an Oxford postgraduate examination, was double-marked with a third marker for deviations over nine points, and gave participants three weeks to complete the take-home assignment.
requirements: Weekly live tutorials with a tutor facilitating discussion
Weekly video lectures watched in preparation for tutorials
constraints: During the pilot, participants had no opportunity to interact with each other outside tutorial sessions due to institutional restrictions on experiments involving minors
target_learning_goals: advanced quantum theory concepts and problem-solving at postgraduate exam level
examples: The exam consisted of three multi-part questions, each progressively increasing in difficulty, adapted from previous Oxford postgraduate exams

article_title: High schoolers excel at Oxford quantum course using pictorial mathematics
citation: Bob Coecke, Aleks Kissinger, Stefano Gogioso, Selma Dündar-Coecke, Caterina Puca, Lia Yeh, Muhammad Hamza Waseem, Emmanuel M. Pothos, Sieglinde Pfaendler, Vincent Wang-Mascianica, Thomas Cervoni, Ferdi Tomassini, Vincent Anandraj, Peter Sigrist and Ilyas Khan. (2025). High schoolers excel at Oxford quantum course using pictorial mathematics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00141
title: Canary and sentinel exam questions for filtering engagement and identifying exceptional mastery
description: The exam embedded two special question types. A two-part 'canary' question was deliberately included "to identify papers where students made very little effort to read the material and answer the questions"; failing it led to the exam being discarded, and correct answers were a prerequisite for passing the assessment. At the other end, Question 3b was described as difficult even in QPic, giving "an indication of which students gained an exceptionally strong grasp of the material", and was referred to as the 'sentinel' question.
requirements: The canary question had two parts, both of which needed correct answers for the exam to count
target_learners: high school students taking the end-of-course assessment
target_learning_goals: basic engagement with course material and exceptional mastery of QPic problem-solving
examples: The canary question (3a.1 and 3a.2) essentially required students to reproduce two definitions given in the course
